newsitem.title: USA: Actor Woody Harrelson faces jail in defending hemp.
newsitem.headline: Actor Woody Harrelson faces jail in defending hemp.

text.p: Actor Woody Harrelson said on Wednesday he planted four marijuana seeds in a stunt to promote hemp as a viable crop and would go to jail if necessary to protest against a Kentucky law barring the plant.

The actor, famous for roles as a bartender in the television series "Cheers" and a crazed killer in the movie "Natural Born Killers," testified at a county court hearing on a misdemeanor marijuana possession charge that could land him a three-month jail term.

"I came to this initially as an environmentalist, now I see it as an important crop issue for farmers," Harrelson testified. "One hundred and fifty years ago hemp was the leading cash crop in Kentucky, and in my mind I don't see any reason why that can't be the case again."

In June, Harrelson bought one acre (0.5 hectares) of land near Booneville and planted four French hemp seeds -- one less than the five seeds which constitute a felony -- expressly to challenge the Kentucky law.
Kentucky, one of the leading states for growing marijuana, also bans hemp, a form of the plant that contains only a tiny fraction of the drug that gives marijuana smokers a "high."

Harrelson said that with growing opposition to cigarettes, Kentucky tobacco farmers could profit by switching to hemp, which could be substituted for trees in making paper and be used to create clothing and other products.

Lee County Judge Ralph McClahan said he would take 90 days to decide whether to grant Harrelson's motion to dismiss the charges, with the understanding any ruling may be appealed to challenge the state's law that bans all forms of marijuana.

Harrelson owns a company in California, Hempstead Co., which sells hemp-based products. The company had about $1.5 million in sales last year but U.S. laws forced suppliers to acquire the raw material from China and elsewhere.

Asked if he was interested in pursuing the legalisation of marijuana in general, Harrelson laughed and said no. "That's not really my concern. In my checkered past, no one I knew ever had any problem acquiring it."

Police who work in drug enforcement testified Wednesday that legalising hemp would make tracking illegal marijuana growers nearly impossible. But Harrelson said he had visited hemp farms in England, Germany and the Netherlands where authorities were able to distinguish between legal and criminal varieties.
